Benefits based on net income. Taxable spousal support raises the recipient’s net income, which is the starting point for the Canada child benefit, the GST/HST credit and many provincial benefits paid from July of the following year. Deductible support lowers the payer’s net income. For a recipient in a benefit phase-out range, the after-tax and after-benefit value of each dollar of spousal support is lower than the tax calculation alone shows. Child support does not count as income for these benefits.

Instalments. No tax is withheld from support payments. A recipient whose taxable support is large relative to tax withheld from other income may owe a balance at filing and may be asked to pay instalments.

Lump sums are generally not periodic and so not deductible or taxable, especially a sum paid to settle future obligations or released rights. Exceptions are arrears of periodic amounts that fell due after the order or agreement, an advance of future periodic support under a court order, and retroactive periodic support for a period before a court order. A lump sum under a written agreement for a period before that agreement does not qualify (Folio ¶3.44–3.46). A recipient of a qualifying retroactive lump sum of CAD 3,000 or more may be able to ask CRA to tax it as if received in the earlier years (Form T1198).

Payments to third parties, such as rent, a mortgage or medical bills paid directly, are deemed paid to the recipient (subsection 60.1(1)) but still need to be a support amount. For specific-purpose payments to count, the order or agreement must say that subsections 60.1(2) and 56.1(2) apply, or clearly state they are taxable to the recipient and deductible by the payer. Payments for a home the payer lives in are excluded, and payments toward buying or improving the recipient’s home are limited to 20% of the original loan principal each year (¶3.50–3.61).

RRSP room. Earned income for RRSP purposes adds taxable support received and subtracts deductible support paid. In the default case, the recipient’s 2027 RRSP room rises by CAD 3,240 (18% of CAD 18,000) and the payer’s falls by the same amount, both subject to the annual dollar limit and each person’s other earned income.
Repaid support: a recipient who repays support under a court order that they earlier reported can deduct the repayment on line 22000 in the year of repayment or either of the two following years.

A payer generally cannot claim the amount for an eligible dependant (line 30400) for a child they must pay support for. In the year a couple separates, though, a payer who meets the line 30400 conditions for the child, for example because the child lived with them before the separation, can choose: deduct the spousal support paid on line 22000, or enter zero there and claim the personal credits (line 30400 and, for that child, lines 30425 and 31800). They cannot have both for the same year.

If the order sets both kinds of support, CRA treats every payment in a year as child support until all child support for that year and earlier years is paid. Only payments above that count as spousal support and can be deducted. Under the paragraph 60(b) formula, the Folio shows the shortfall reducing the deduction dollar for dollar (Example 1).

In the year a couple separates, a payer who meets the line 30400 conditions for the child can claim either the line 30400 credit (and lines 30425 and 31800 for that child) or the support deduction, not both. Here the deduction is worth more once spousal support passes about CAD 11,235. The credit uses CAD 16,452 at 14% for a child with no income and is capped by the payer’s federal tax.

Take a former couple with an order made in 2025. The payer has CAD 110,000 of employment income; the recipient has CAD 35,000 and the children. The order requires CAD 1,000 a month of child support and CAD 1,500 a month of spousal support, and the payer pays all CAD 30,000 in 2026.

The CAD 18,000 deduction stays within the payer’s 20.5% band (CAD 58,523 to 117,045), and the inclusion stays within the recipient’s 14% band, so the two federal returns together pay CAD 1,170 less than if the spousal support were not deductible. Provincial tax adds a similar effect at provincial rates. The first chart shows how the saving and the added tax change with the amount: each moves at the marginal rate of the person concerned, so the net effect shrinks or reverses when the recipient has the higher income or the support pushes them into a higher bracket.

The date matters because orders made before May 1997 followed the older rule, under which child support was deductible and taxable too. Such an order moves to the current rules if the child support is changed after April 1997, if a new order between the same people changes the total, if the order names a date from which the new rules apply, or if both parties sign Form T1157. The election cannot be reversed. This guide models current-rule orders only.

The line 30400 credit for a child with no income is CAD 16,452 at 14%, or CAD 2,303.28. The deduction is worth the payer’s marginal federal rate on the spousal support paid. At CAD 110,000 of income, that is 20.5% until the deduction carries the payer below CAD 58,523, so the deduction wins once spousal support passes about CAD 11,235. A payer paying CAD 8,000 of spousal support would save CAD 1,640 by deducting it and CAD 2,303.28 with the credit. The choice affects only the payer’s return: the recipient still includes the spousal support. The fifth chart shows the crossover for the incomes entered; provincial credits and rates change it in practice.

The model uses 2026 federal brackets and treats net income as taxable income, with the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered. It assumes an order made after April 1997, periodic payments the recipient controls, one recipient, and that the CRA registration and living-apart conditions are met. Provincial and territorial tax, other credits, income-tested benefits and Quebec’s separate system are not included, and it does not decide how much support is owed. Use tax software, a family lawyer or a tax professional for an actual case.

The payer deducts at their own marginal federal rate and the recipient pays at theirs, so the net change depends on the gap between the two brackets. With the payer at CAD 110,000 and the recipient at CAD 35,000 of net income before support, each dollar moves between the two returns until it pushes the recipient into a higher bracket or the payer into a lower one. Two kinds of support, two tax results

Under Folio S1-F3-C3 (¶3.13), any amount the order does not identify as solely for the spouse or former spouse is a child support amount. A single global figure “for the family” is therefore treated entirely as child support, with no deduction. Spousal support has to be stated separately to be deductible.

Under orders and agreements made after April 1997, child support is paid from the payer’s after-tax income and arrives tax-free. Spousal support stated separately in the order is deductible by the payer on line 22000 and taxable to the recipient on line 12800, but each year’s payments count first as child support, so a payer who falls behind loses the spousal deduction until all child support is caught up. The deduction is worth the payer’s marginal rate and the tax is the recipient’s, so the net federal effect depends on the gap between their two brackets.
